definition: A set of people, processes, data, and technology that collects, stores, and delivers information to support a business activity.
wrongs: A single laptop, considered apart from people, data, and working methods.
A paper company logo with no data and no process behind it.
The building's electrical wiring diagram alone.
why: An information system combines people, process, data, and technology in support of a business activity.
example: A shop's till, stock database, cashiers, and reorder rules together form the sales information system.
scenario: A manager describes only the new server and ignores staff, data, and the sales process. Which label is incomplete?
scenarioAnswer: Calling the server alone the information system
scenarioWrongs: Including people, data, process, and technology
Using the till data to reorder stock
Training cashiers to follow the sales steps
scenarioWhy: An information system is the combination of people, process, data, and technology, not the server by itself.

definition: A system that captures and processes routine business events, such as sales or payments, as they occur.
wrongs: A tool used only by senior executives to scan a handful of strategic charts once a quarter.
A library of past project essays kept for students to read.
A drawing package used to design a company logo.
why: Transaction processing systems exist to record high-volume routine events accurately and immediately.
example: Each card payment in a supermarket is recorded at the till so stock and cash figures update at once.
scenario: The business needs every card payment recorded as it happens so stock stays correct. Which system type fits?
scenarioWrongs: A quarterly executive chart pack only
scenarioWhy: Recording routine events such as payments as they occur is the job of a transaction processing system.

definition: A system that summarises operational data into regular reports managers use to monitor and control performance.
wrongs: A system whose only job is to capture each sale at the moment it happens.
A robot that replaces every manager with no reports at all.
A social network used for personal photos.
why: A management information system turns operational data into routine reports for monitoring, rather than only posting transactions.
example: Each Monday a store manager receives a report of last week's sales by department, drawn from till data.
scenario: Store managers want a weekly summary of sales by department, not a live till. Which system type fits?
scenarioWrongs: A system that only prints receipts at the till
A robot that issues no reports
scenarioWhy: Summarising operational data into regular management reports is the role of a management information system.

definition: A system that combines data and models so a person can compare options for a decision that is not fully routine.
wrongs: A system that posts each invoice automatically with no analysis of choices.
A fixed monthly report that never lets the user try alternative assumptions.
A lock on a server room door.
why: Decision support helps a person explore alternatives with data and models when the decision is semi-structured.
example: A planner uses a tool to compare three staffing plans under different sales forecasts before hiring temporary staff.
scenario: A planner must compare three staffing plans under different forecasts before hiring. Which system type fits?
scenarioWrongs: An automatic invoice poster with no comparison
A fixed report that cannot change assumptions
scenarioWhy: Comparing options with data and models for a non-routine choice is decision support.

definition: A visual display of a small set of key indicators that senior managers use to see organisational performance quickly.
wrongs: A dump of every raw transaction row from the last ten years.
A source-code editor for application developers.
A paper form used to apply for annual leave.
why: An executive dashboard concentrates a few important indicators into a visual view for senior oversight.
example: The chief operating officer opens one screen showing this month's revenue, complaints, and on-time delivery.
scenario: A director wants one screen with revenue, complaints, and on-time delivery, not raw rows. Which tool fits?
scenarioWrongs: A ten-year dump of every transaction row
scenarioWhy: An executive dashboard shows a few key indicators visually so a senior manager can see performance quickly.

definition: An integrated suite that shares one set of data across core functions such as finance, human resources, procurement, and inventory.
wrongs: A single spreadsheet kept privately by one department and never linked to finance.
A customer chat widget that only answers frequently asked questions.
A standalone game installed on a reception PC.
why: Enterprise resource planning integrates core business functions on shared data so the organisation does not run them as isolated systems.
example: When goods are received, the same system updates inventory, the purchase order, and the supplier balance in finance.
scenario: Receiving goods must update stock, the purchase order, and the supplier balance together. Which system type fits?
scenarioWrongs: A private spreadsheet in one department
A game on the reception PC
scenarioWhy: Enterprise resource planning shares one data set across functions such as inventory, purchasing, and finance.

definition: A system that records customer interactions and supports sales, marketing, and service so relationships can be managed consistently.
wrongs: A payroll system whose only records are staff salaries.
A tool that tracks raw materials inside a warehouse and never stores customer contacts.
A firewall that blocks network ports.
why: Customer relationship management keeps a shared view of customers and supports sales, marketing, and service work.
example: A service agent sees a customer's open orders and last three calls before answering a complaint.
scenario: Service staff need the customer's orders and recent calls on one screen before answering a complaint. Which system fits?
scenarioWrongs: A warehouse materials tracker with no customer records
scenarioWhy: Customer relationship management stores interactions so sales and service share one view of the customer.

definition: Software that coordinates the flow of materials, information, and money from suppliers through operations to customers.
wrongs: A tool that only stores employee holiday requests.
A word processor used to write the annual report.
A badge reader that only opens the front door.
why: Supply chain systems coordinate flows across suppliers, the organisation, and customers, not internal HR tasks.
example: A manufacturer uses one system to align supplier deliveries, factory schedules, and retailer orders.
scenario: Supplier deliveries, the factory schedule, and retailer orders must be planned together. Which system type fits?
scenarioWhy: Supply chain management coordinates materials, information, and orders from suppliers through to customers.

definition: A system that captures, stores, and shares organisational knowledge so staff can find and reuse it.
wrongs: A till that only records the price of each sale.
A payroll calculator with no articles, guides, or lessons learned.
A door alarm that sounds when left open.
why: Knowledge management systems exist so expertise and documents can be found and reused, rather than remaining with one person.
example: Engineers search a maintained wiki for the approved way to reset a production line before calling a retiree.
scenario: New engineers need the approved reset steps without calling a retired expert. Which system type fits?
scenarioWhy: A knowledge management system stores and shares organisational know-how so others can reuse it.

definition: A set of linked activities that turns inputs into a result of value to a customer or the organisation.
wrongs: A single unconnected mouse click with no input or result.
The brand colour chosen for a website header.
A staff member's home address.
why: A business process is the linked work that converts inputs into a valued output, not an isolated click or a colour choice.
example: Order fulfilment links taking the order, picking stock, packing, shipping, and confirming delivery.
scenario: Taking an order, picking stock, packing, and shipping are linked to deliver a parcel. Which term covers that chain?
scenarioWrongs: One mouse click with no output
scenarioWhy: A business process is the linked set of activities that produces a valued result, such as a delivered order.

definition: A diagram that shows the steps, decisions, and hand-offs in a business process.
wrongs: A street map of the city where the office stands.
A list of employee birthdays.
A photograph of the chief executive.
why: A process map is a diagram of how work flows, including decisions and hand-offs, not a geographical map.
example: A team draws the refund process, including who approves amounts over a set limit.
scenario: Staff disagree about who approves large refunds. Which artefact should show the steps and the decision?
scenarioWrongs: A portrait of the chief executive
scenarioWhy: A process map diagrams steps, decisions, and hand-offs so the refund approval path is visible.

definition: A description of how work is actually done today, including current delays and workarounds.
wrongs: A picture of the ideal process after a future system is installed.
A slogan about the company's hopes for next year.
A list of features the vendor wishes the product had.
why: The as-is process records current practice, including its problems, before improvement is designed.
example: Analysts watch clerks retype invoices from email because the current system cannot import them.
scenario: Before buying software, analysts watch clerks retype invoices from email. Which description are they capturing?
scenarioWrongs: The future process after the new system
scenarioWhy: Watching how invoices are handled today, including the retyping workaround, captures the as-is process.

definition: A description of how a process should work after a planned improvement or system change.
wrongs: A photograph of the queues and workarounds that exist this morning.
An unrelated historical novel about the industry.
The resignations submitted last year.
why: The to-be process is the intended future way of working, used to guide design and change.
example: The redesigned claim process shows customers uploading documents once, instead of posting paper copies.
scenario: The design shows customers uploading a claim once, replacing today's paper copies. Which description is that?
scenarioWhy: The intended future way of working, after the change, is the to-be process.

definition: The person accountable for the performance and improvement of a named business process.
wrongs: A visitor who uses the process once and then leaves.
A server that stores the process diagram.
Every employee equally, with nobody accountable.
why: A process owner is the named person accountable for how well that process performs and how it improves.
example: The head of admissions is accountable for the application process, including its cycle time and error rate.
scenario: Cycle time for applications is poor, and someone must be accountable for improving that process. Which role is that?
scenarioWrongs: Nobody, because everyone is equally accountable
scenarioWhy: The process owner is the person accountable for the performance and improvement of that named process.

definition: A comparison of current performance or capability with a desired target, used to identify what must change.
wrongs: A celebration of targets that ignores the current state.
A random list of software brands with no target.
Copying last year's plan without comparing it to today's capability.
why: Gap analysis identifies the difference between where the organisation is and where it needs to be.
example: A clinic finds it can book 40 appointments a day but needs 70, and lists the shortfall in staff and system time.
scenario: A clinic can book 40 visits a day and needs 70. Which analysis names that shortfall and what must change?
scenarioWrongs: A party for meeting the target
A brand list with no comparison
scenarioWhy: Gap analysis compares the current 40 visits with the needed 70 and identifies what must change.

definition: A person or group that can affect, or is affected by, a business or system decision.
wrongs: Only the programmer who writes the final line of code.
A person with no interest and no influence over the decision.
The brand of keyboard used in the office.
why: Stakeholders are people or groups with influence on a decision or who feel its effects.
example: For a new billing system, customers, finance staff, and the regulator are all treated as stakeholders.
scenario: A new billing system will change what customers pay and what finance staff do, and a regulator sets rules. Who should be treated as stakeholders?
scenarioAnswer: Customers, finance staff, and the regulator
scenarioWrongs: Only the last programmer to commit code
People with no interest and no influence
scenarioWhy: Stakeholders include those affected, such as customers and staff, and those who can affect the decision, such as a regulator.

definition: A senior manager who authorises a change, secures resources, and is accountable for its business outcome.
wrongs: A contractor hired only to install a printer on one afternoon.
A student observer with no authority over budget or scope.
The software vendor's sales brochure.
why: The business sponsor owns the outcome and provides authority and resources, rather than merely observing.
example: The finance director sponsors the billing replacement, approves its budget, and answers for the expected savings.
scenario: Someone must approve the budget for a billing replacement and answer for the savings. Which role is that?
scenarioWhy: The business sponsor authorises the change, secures resources, and is accountable for the business outcome.

definition: A statement of what the organisation needs to achieve, written in business terms rather than as a technical design.
wrongs: A choice of programming language made by a developer.
The colour of a server status LED.
A line of source code that implements a loop.
why: A business requirement states a business need, leaving technical design choices to a later step.
example: The business requires that a customer can receive a correct invoice within one day of delivery.
scenario: The organisation needs customers to receive a correct invoice within one day of delivery. Which kind of statement is that?
scenarioWrongs: The colour of a status LED
scenarioWhy: A need stated in business terms, such as invoice timing, is a business requirement rather than a technical design.

definition: A statement of a behaviour the system must provide, such as recording an order or producing an invoice.
wrongs: A limit on response time, availability, or security that does not name a behaviour.
The project budget approved by the board.
The brand font used on posters.
why: A functional requirement states a behaviour the system must perform, not a quality level or a budget.
example: The system must let a clerk record a refund and notify the customer by email.
scenario: The statement says the system must record a refund and email the customer. Which kind of requirement is that?
scenarioWrongs: A response-time limit with no behaviour named
scenarioWhy: Recording a refund and sending an email are behaviours the system must provide, so the statement is functional.

definition: A statement of a quality the system must meet, such as response time, availability, security, or usability.
wrongs: A statement that the system must provide a named function, such as creating an order.
The name of the project sponsor.
A list of office furniture to be purchased.
why: A non-functional requirement states how well the system must perform, not which business function it offers.
example: The checkout page must return a confirmation within two seconds for 95 percent of requests.
scenario: Checkout confirmation must appear within two seconds for 95 percent of requests. Which kind of requirement is that?
scenarioWrongs: A functional requirement to create an order
scenarioWhy: A response-time target is a quality the system must meet, so it is a non-functional requirement.

definition: A plan that sets how technology investments will support the organisation's goals over several years.
wrongs: A list of this morning's help-desk tickets.
A one-off password reset for a single user.
The canteen menu for the current week.
why: IT strategy is a multi-year plan linking technology investment to organisational goals, not daily support work.
example: A university's IT strategy commits five years of investment to online enrolment because growth in remote students is a goal.
scenario: Leaders must decide five years of technology investment to support growth in remote students. Which plan is that?
scenarioWhy: IT strategy sets how technology investment will support business goals over several years.

definition: The fit between IT projects and the organisation's stated business objectives.
wrongs: Buying every new device because it is fashionable, with no link to objectives.
Aligning office desks so they face the same direction.
Making the IT budget exactly equal to the marketing budget by coincidence.
why: Strategic alignment means IT work is chosen because it supports stated business objectives.
example: A proposed game server is rejected because the firm's stated objective is faster insurance claims, which the server does not serve.
scenario: A proposed system does not support any stated business objective. Which judgement follows from strategic alignment?
scenarioAnswer: It is a poor fit and should not be a priority
scenarioWrongs: It should be bought because it is new
It aligns because the desks face one way
It aligns because two budgets happen to match
scenarioWhy: Strategic alignment requires an IT project to fit stated business objectives, so an unrelated system is a poor priority.

definition: A structured review of internal strengths and weaknesses and of external opportunities and threats.
wrongs: A test that only measures the speed of a computer processor.
A contract clause about late payment.
A count of chairs in a meeting room.
why: SWOT examines internal strengths and weaknesses together with external opportunities and threats.
example: Before moving sales online, a retailer lists its strong brand, weak delivery IT, a new market, and a large online rival.
scenario: A retailer lists a strong brand, weak delivery IT, a new market, and a powerful online rival. Which analysis is that?
scenarioWhy: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats are the four parts of a SWOT analysis.

definition: A durable edge that lets an organisation outperform rivals, which information systems may support but do not guarantee.
wrongs: Any purchase of software, which automatically makes a firm unbeatable.
A one-day price cut that rivals copy the next morning.
Having more chairs than a neighbouring office.
why: Competitive advantage is a lasting performance edge; technology can support it but does not create it automatically.
example: A carrier's routing system keeps delivery promises rivals cannot match, and customers stay because of that reliability.
scenario: Rivals copy a one-day discount overnight, but they still cannot match your reliable routing system. Which item is the competitive advantage?
scenarioAnswer: The durable delivery reliability rivals cannot match
scenarioWrongs: The one-day discount they copied immediately
The mere fact that software was purchased
scenarioWhy: Competitive advantage is a durable edge rivals cannot quickly copy, not a short-lived discount or a purchase by itself.

definition: The sequence of primary and support activities through which an organisation creates value for its customers.
wrongs: A metal chain used to lock bicycles outside the office.
The order of slides in a sales presentation only.
A list of shareholders and their voting weights.
why: The value chain describes the activities that create customer value, including both primary work and support activities.
example: A manufacturer's value chain links inbound parts, production, outbound delivery, marketing, and after-sales service.
scenario: Leaders trace how parts, production, delivery, marketing, and service together create what customers pay for. Which model is that?
scenarioWrongs: The slide order in a pitch deck
scenarioWhy: The value chain is the set of primary and support activities that create what the customer values.

definition: A significant change in how an organisation uses digital technology to alter its processes, products, or customer experience.
wrongs: Replacing one broken keyboard with the same model.
Scanning a single paper letter without changing the service.
Renaming the IT department without changing any process.
why: Digital transformation changes how the organisation works or what it offers, not a like-for-like equipment swap.
example: A bank replaces branch-only account opening with a fully online journey and redesigns the roles of branch staff.
scenario: A bank moves account opening fully online and redesigns branch jobs. Which description fits that change?
scenarioWrongs: Replacing one keyboard with the same model
Scanning one letter and leaving the service unchanged
scenarioWhy: Changing the customer journey and the related jobs through digital technology is digital transformation.

definition: A choice between building a system in-house and purchasing or subscribing to an existing product.
wrongs: A choice between two colours for the office walls.
A decision to hire or fire a particular receptionist.
A choice of sandwich fillings for a meeting.
why: Make-or-buy compares building a capability internally with acquiring an existing product or service.
example: A charity compares building its own donor system with subscribing to an established fundraising platform.
scenario: A charity can build a donor system or subscribe to an existing platform. Which decision is that?
scenarioWhy: Choosing between an in-house build and an existing product is a make-or-buy decision.

definition: A documented argument that compares the expected benefits, costs, and risks of a proposed investment.
wrongs: A suitcase used to carry a laptop to a client site.
A username and password for a finance system.
A poster advertising an existing product.
why: A business case is the written justification of an investment, weighing benefits, costs, and risks.
example: The board reads a case showing that a new roster system costs less over five years than continued overtime.
scenario: The board wants the costs, benefits, and risks of a roster system before approving money. Which document should they read?
scenarioWrongs: An advert for a current product
scenarioWhy: A business case documents the expected benefits, costs, and risks of the proposed investment.

definition: A comparison of the expected costs of an option with its expected benefits, expressed in money where that is possible.
wrongs: A list of benefits with every cost left out.
A list of costs with every benefit ignored.
A vote based only on which option has the nicest name.
why: Cost-benefit analysis puts expected costs and expected benefits side by side so an option can be judged.
example: An options paper shows a portal costs 80,000 and is expected to save 30,000 a year in postage.
scenario: One option costs 80,000 and is expected to save 30,000 a year. Which technique sets those figures side by side?
scenarioWrongs: Choosing the option with the nicest name
scenarioWhy: Cost-benefit analysis compares expected costs with expected benefits for the option.

definition: A measure of the net gain from an investment relative to its cost, often expressed as a percentage.
wrongs: The number of people who attended the project launch party.
The physical distance between two offices.
The count of slides in a presentation.
why: Return on investment relates net gain to the cost of the investment so options can be compared.
example: A 100,000 system that returns 20,000 net per year is described as having a 20 percent annual return on investment.
scenario: A 100,000 system returns 20,000 net in a year. Which measure states that gain relative to the cost?
scenarioWhy: Return on investment expresses net gain relative to investment cost, here 20,000 on 100,000.

definition: The full cost of owning a system over its life, including purchase, operation, support, training, and retirement.
wrongs: The sticker price alone, ignoring support, training, and running costs.
Only the cost of electricity on the first day.
The salary of the chief executive, unrelated to the system.
why: Total cost of ownership includes the whole life cost, not just the initial purchase price.
example: A cheap printer is rejected after toner, maintenance, and downtime costs exceed a dearer model over four years.
scenario: A cheap printer has high toner, maintenance, and downtime costs over four years. Which figure should drive the choice?
scenarioWhy: Total cost of ownership adds purchase, running, support, and retirement costs over the system's life.

definition: The time needed for the net benefits of an investment to recover its initial cost.
wrongs: The time a vendor takes to answer a sales email.
The length of the chief executive's employment contract.
The number of years the company has existed.
why: Payback period is how long cumulative net benefits take to cover the initial outlay.
example: A 60,000 kiosk that saves 20,000 net each year has a payback period of three years.
scenario: A 60,000 kiosk saves 20,000 net each year. How long is the payback period?
scenarioWhy: Payback is initial cost divided by annual net benefit, so 60,000 divided by 20,000 is three years.

definition: An expected gain that is real but hard to price reliably, such as better morale or a stronger reputation.
wrongs: A saving that is already measured as fewer overtime hours with a known wage rate.
A cash refund received from a supplier.
A reduction in licence fees stated on an invoice.
why: Intangible benefits matter but cannot be priced with the same confidence as a measured cash saving.
example: A portal is expected to improve the council's reputation, but the team cannot honestly attach a firm cash value.
scenario: A portal should improve public reputation, but no reliable cash value can be given. Which label fits that gain?
scenarioWrongs: A measured overtime saving at a known wage
A licence-fee cut printed on an invoice
scenarioWhy: A real gain that cannot be priced reliably, such as reputation, is an intangible benefit.

definition: An expected gain that can be measured in money, such as reduced overtime cost or fewer lost sales.
wrongs: A feeling that the brand seems more modern, with no measurable cash effect.
A hope that staff will be happier, with no agreed measure.
A rumour that customers like the new colour.
why: A tangible benefit can be expressed in money from a stated measure, unlike a vague improvement in feeling.
example: Cutting failed deliveries by 200 a month, at a known cost of 15 each, is entered as a cash saving.
scenario: Failed deliveries fall by 200 a month and each failure costs 15. Which label fits that monthly saving?
scenarioWrongs: An unpriced feeling that the brand is modern
A hope about morale with no measure
A rumour about a popular colour
scenarioWhy: A gain that can be priced, here 200 failures times 15, is a tangible benefit.

definition: An early assessment of whether a proposal is technically, economically, legally, and operationally workable.
wrongs: The final user manual written after the system has already gone live.
A party to celebrate a completed project.
A decision to skip all investigation and start coding immediately.
why: A feasibility study checks, before major commitment, whether the proposal can work on technical, economic, legal, and operational grounds.
example: A hospital study finds a proposed app would breach a records law, so the project stops before build.
scenario: Before spending build money, a hospital checks whether an app is legal, affordable, and operable. Which study is that?
scenarioWrongs: The final user manual after go-live
Starting to code with no investigation
scenarioWhy: An early check of technical, economic, legal, and operational workability is a feasibility study.

definition: The structured approach to preparing and supporting people so they adopt a new process or system.
wrongs: A technical patch that changes source code while ignoring the people who must use it.
A ban on ever altering a process, even when the business requires it.
The version history inside a code repository alone.
why: Change management focuses on people adopting the new way of working, not only on the technical change.
example: Before a new roster goes live, supervisors are briefed, staff are trained, and floor support is rostered for the first month.
scenario: A new roster will fail if supervisors and staff do not adopt it. Which work prepares and supports those people?
scenarioWrongs: A code patch that ignores users
A ban on all process change
scenarioWhy: Change management prepares and supports people so they actually adopt the new roster.

definition: Reluctance to adopt a new system or process, often from fear of lost skill, extra work, or an unclear benefit.
wrongs: Enthusiastic early use of a system people already trust.
A measured technical defect that stops the software starting.
A legal prohibition that makes the change unlawful.
why: Resistance is human reluctance to adopt a change, and it is different from a technical fault or a legal ban.
example: Experienced clerks avoid a new system because they fear looking slow, so they keep private spreadsheets.
scenario: Clerks keep old spreadsheets because they fear looking slow on the new system, which itself works. Which issue is that?
scenarioWrongs: A software crash that prevents login
A law that forbids the process
Eager adoption by staff who already trust the tool
scenarioWhy: Avoiding a working system from fear of lost standing is resistance to change, not a technical failure.

definition: A respected staff member who promotes a change locally and helps colleagues adopt it.
wrongs: A person who blocks every change without offering a reason.
An external celebrity with no role in the workplace.
A printed poster that nobody is asked to support.
why: A change champion is a trusted insider who actively helps colleagues take up the new way of working.
example: A respected nurse shows the ward how the new drug chart works and answers questions during the first shifts.
scenario: A respected nurse demonstrates the new chart and helps colleagues on the first shifts. Which role is that?
scenarioWrongs: A person who blocks the change with no reason
An external celebrity with no workplace role
scenarioWhy: A change champion is a respected colleague who promotes the change and helps others adopt it.

definition: A study that identifies the skills people lack for a new process or system and the learning required to close that gap.
wrongs: A count of how many chairs a training room can hold, with no look at skills.
A decision to buy software with no thought about who must learn it.
A list of everyone's favourite hobbies.
why: Training needs analysis compares required skills with current skills so the right learning can be planned.
example: Before go-live, a bank finds cashiers can take cash but cannot reverse a card payment, and schedules that lesson.
scenario: Cashiers cannot reverse card payments on the new till, and that skill is required. Which study should find and plan that lesson?
scenarioWrongs: A count of chairs in the room
scenarioWhy: Training needs analysis identifies the missing skill and the learning needed before the new till is used.

definition: The ongoing work of checking whether the benefits promised in the business case actually occur after the change.
wrongs: Writing hopeful benefits in a case and never measuring them later.
Celebrating approval of the budget as if the benefits had already arrived.
Counting the number of logos on the project slides.
why: Benefits realisation tracks promised benefits after go-live and acts if they are not appearing.
example: Six months after launch, finance checks whether postage savings in the business case have actually occurred.
scenario: Six months after launch, finance checks whether the promised postage savings happened. Which activity is that?
scenarioWrongs: Writing benefits and never looking again
Treating budget approval as if savings already exist
scenarioWhy: Benefits realisation measures whether the savings promised in the case have actually occurred after launch.

definition: A quantified measure that shows how well an important business objective is being achieved.
wrongs: A vague slogan such as be the best, with no measure.
A count of unrelated office plants.
The name of the objective with no number attached.
why: A key performance indicator is a number tied to an important objective so performance can be judged.
example: A support team tracks the percentage of tickets resolved within one working day against a target of 90 percent.
scenario: The objective is fast support, and the team tracks the percentage of tickets closed within one day. Which label fits that measure?
scenarioWhy: A quantified measure of an important objective, such as same-day resolution rate, is a key performance indicator.

definition: A choice based primarily on relevant and reliable evidence rather than on habit or unsupported opinion.
wrongs: A choice made because it matches the loudest opinion in the room, with the data unread.
A choice copied from last year without checking whether conditions changed.
A choice based on a rumour in a corridor.
why: A data-driven decision gives relevant, reliable evidence the leading role in the choice.
example: A retailer opens evening hours only in stores where sales data show demand after 6 p.m., not in every branch by habit.
scenario: Evening opening is proposed for every store by habit, but sales data show demand after 6 p.m. in only some branches. Which decision is data-driven?
scenarioAnswer: Open evenings only where the sales data show demand
scenarioWrongs: Open every store because that is last year's habit
Follow the loudest opinion and ignore the data
Act on a corridor rumour about one shop
scenarioWhy: A data-driven decision follows the relevant sales evidence about where evening demand actually exists.

definition: The fitness of data for its intended use, including accuracy, completeness, timeliness, and consistency.
wrongs: The size of the database server, regardless of whether the figures are wrong.
The artistic layout of a report that hides missing values.
The number of colours in a dashboard theme.
why: Data quality is whether data are fit to use, judged by properties such as accuracy, completeness, timeliness, and consistency.
example: A mailing is postponed because 30 percent of customer postcodes are blank, so the addresses are not fit to use.
scenario: Thirty percent of postcodes are blank, so labels would go to the wrong places. Which problem is that?
scenarioWrongs: A server that is too small but holds correct addresses
A dull colour theme on a correct report
A complete and current address file
scenarioWhy: Missing postcodes mean the address data are not complete enough for the mailing, which is a data-quality failure.

definition: Core business entities, such as customers, products, and suppliers, that are shared across systems and should stay consistent.
wrongs: A one-off social message that is never reused.
The temperature reading from a sensor at a single moment, kept only in that device.
A temporary password that expires in one hour.
why: Master data are the shared core records of the business, such as who the customers and products are.
example: Customer name and account number are maintained once and reused by billing, support, and marketing.
scenario: Billing, support, and marketing must use the same customer name and account number. Which data are those?
scenarioWrongs: A password that expires in an hour
scenarioWhy: Shared core entities such as customers, kept consistent across systems, are master data.

definition: One authoritative store for a given data item so teams do not act on conflicting copies.
wrongs: Several spreadsheets that staff update separately and then argue over.
A rule that every person keeps a private version and none is official.
Printing the same report from three different unofficial files.
why: A single source of truth means one agreed place holds the authoritative value for that data item.
example: All departments read product price from the product master, and local price spreadsheets are withdrawn.
scenario: Two teams quote different prices because each edits its own spreadsheet. Which fix creates a single source of truth?
scenarioAnswer: Make one product master the only authoritative price
scenarioWrongs: Let every team keep a private price and call them all official
Email conflicting prices and let staff guess
scenarioWhy: A single source of truth is one authoritative store, so teams stop acting on conflicting copies.

definition: Tools and practices that turn organisational data into reports and analyses used for management decisions.
wrongs: The human ability to score well on an IQ test, unrelated to business data.
A transaction screen used only to type in one sale.
A spam filter on the chief executive's mailbox.
why: Business intelligence is the reporting and analysis of organisational data to support decisions.
example: Managers explore a report of profit by region and product to decide which line to expand.
scenario: Managers need to explore profit by region and product before choosing a line to expand. Which capability fits?
scenarioWrongs: A screen that only types in one sale
scenarioWhy: Turning organisational data into analysis for a management decision is business intelligence.

definition: A subject-oriented store of integrated historical data, kept for analysis rather than for moment-by-moment transactions.
wrongs: The live till system that must post each sale in real time.
A cupboard of blank paper forms.
A chat channel used for today's operational instructions.
why: A data warehouse integrates history for analysis and is not the system that posts live transactions.
example: Nightly sales from many shops are loaded into one warehouse so analysts can compare five years of trends.
scenario: Analysts need five years of sales from many shops, integrated for trends, without querying the live tills. Which store fits?
scenarioWhy: A data warehouse holds integrated historical data for analysis, separate from live transaction processing.

definition: A system that runs day-to-day transactions and is organised for current processing rather than for long-term analysis.
wrongs: A historical warehouse designed for multi-year trend reports rather than posting today's sales.
A printed strategy covering the next five years.
An archive of retired marketing posters.
why: An operational system processes current business events, whereas analytical stores are built for history and reporting.
example: The reservations system records today's bookings and must stay available during opening hours.
scenario: Staff must record today's bookings as they happen during opening hours. Which system type fits?
scenarioWrongs: A historical warehouse meant only for trend reports
scenarioWhy: Recording current transactions as they happen is the job of an operational system.

definition: An older system that is still required for operations but is costly or risky to change and poorly linked to newer tools.
wrongs: A system launched last week on a current platform with full support.
A paper notebook that was never part of operations.
A future design that has not been built.
why: A legacy system is old but still operational, and it is typically hard to change or integrate.
example: Payroll still runs on a twenty-year-old application that few staff can modify and that cannot feed the new finance suite.
scenario: Payroll still depends on a twenty-year-old application that is risky to modify and cannot feed the new finance suite. Which term fits?
scenarioWrongs: A personal notebook never used in operations
A design that has not been built
scenarioWhy: An old operational system that is hard to change and poorly integrated is a legacy system.

definition: The decision rights and accountability framework that directs how technology is evaluated, directed, and monitored against business goals.
wrongs: A single technician choosing every corporate system with no oversight.
The physical guard rota at the data-centre door, with no decision rights.
A ban on writing down who may approve IT spending.
why: IT governance sets who decides, who is accountable, and how IT is monitored so it serves business goals.
example: A board committee must approve any IT project over a set amount and reviews benefits twice a year.
scenario: Nobody knows who may approve large IT spend, and projects ignore business goals. Which missing framework addresses that?
scenarioWrongs: One technician choosing everything with no oversight
A rule against recording decision rights
scenarioWhy: IT governance defines decision rights and accountability so technology is directed toward business goals.
